Path-Coupled Bellman Flows for Distributional Reinforcement Learning

A flow-matching critic that learns full return distributions on Bellman paths that start at the noise prior, end at the Bellman target, and share their noise with the successor flow.

Boyang Xu, Qing Zou, Siqin Yang, Hao Yan

School of Computing and Augmented Intelligence, Arizona State University

Published at ICML 2026, Seoul

Read the paper Code on GitHub Cite
one noise draw X0 successor path, ends at X′ current path, ends at R + γX′ Point at a path to follow one noise draw

Why return distributions, and why flows

Distributional reinforcement learning trains the critic to predict the whole distribution of returns rather than only their average. Two actions can share an expected return and still carry very different risk, and only the distribution tells them apart. Modelling the full law gives a richer picture of uncertainty, often improves empirical performance, and is the information that risk-sensitive control needs.

Most practical distributional critics, however, still represent that distribution on a fixed grid of atoms or quantile levels. Because a Bellman backup rarely lands on those grid points, every update needs a projection step, which introduces bias and limits how expressive the learned distribution can be.

Flow matching removes the grid. A learned velocity field transports Gaussian noise into return samples, so the critic can represent a continuous return law of any shape. Moreover, the distributional Bellman equation is itself a statement about transport: the return at (s,a)(s,a)(s,a) is an affine image of the successor return,

Zπ(s,a)  =d  R(s,a)+γ Zπ(S′,A′).Z^{\pi}(s,a) \;\overset{d}{=}\; R(s,a) + \gamma\, Z^{\pi}(S', A').Zπ(s,a)=dR(s,a)+γZπ(S′,A′).

Placing that equation inside a flow is nevertheless harder than it looks, because two things break as soon as one tries.

The path starts in the wrong place

Imposing the Bellman map at every flow time gives the pointwise path ZtD=R+γZt′Z^{D}_{t} = R + \gamma Z'_{t}ZtD​=R+γZt′​. It reaches the Bellman target at t=1t = 1t=1, but it starts at R+γX0R + \gamma X_0R+γX0​ instead of the base prior X0∼N(0,1)X_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)X0​∼N(0,1), so it is no longer a valid flow-matching path.

Independent noise makes targets noisy

If the current and successor flows draw their own noise, their trajectories are unrelated between t=0t = 0t=0 and t=1t = 1t=1. Bellman consistency can then be enforced only at the endpoint, and every per-sample target inherits the full randomness of the bootstrapped successor return, which destabilises critic learning.

Where existing critics leave the gap

Prior work has fixed parts of this picture. The table summarises what each family represents and what it leaves open, following the paper's related-work discussion.

ApproachHow returns are representedWhat remains open
Categorical and quantile criticsC51, QR-DQN, IQN, D4PG, CODACFixed atoms or quantile levelsBellman targets rarely land on the grid, so projection steps add bias and cap expressivity.
Endpoint-matched flow criticsValue Flows, DFC, Bellman DiffusionFlows from noise, with the Bellman target matched at the endpoint using independently sampled noiseNo pathwise coupling, so per-sample targets are high-variance. A literal full-ttt Bellman constraint conflicts with the Gaussian source; Value Flows mitigates this with BCFM anchoring.
Temporal-difference flowsTD-FlowFlow over a process that terminates at each step with probability 1−γ1-\gamma1−γApplied to rewards, it models a random-horizon return that matches the discounted return in expectation but generally not in distribution.
Quantile-coupled flowsFlowIQNSorts source and Bellman-target samples within each minibatchRepairs the endpoint coupling rather than the time-continuous path; complementary to PCBF.
Flow-parameterised scalar criticsFloQNoise integrated into a scalar Q-valueScales compute for value estimation but does not model the return distribution.
Path-Coupled Bellman Flowsthis workFlow on a source-consistent Bellman path whose current and successor flows share noiseStarts at the prior, ends at the Bellman target, stays coupled pathwise, and reduces target variance through a λ control variate.

Why closing it matters

Return laws you can trust

On environments with known return laws, PCBF has the lowest Wasserstein error in five of six settings, while an endpoint-consistency baseline degrades as its consistency weight grows, for example 0.586 against 6.856 on the Discrete MC chain at S=5S = 5S=5.

See the toy results

Bootstrapping without the noise

The λ-target lowers the variance of the regression target. Under shared noise its bias scales like (1−γ)(1−t)(1-\gamma)(1-t)(1−γ)(1−t) in the linear–Gaussian analysis, so it shrinks in the long-horizon regime where bootstrap variance hurts most.

Explore the trade-off

Control from full return laws

On 38 offline RL tasks from OGBench and D4RL, PCBF is within 95% of the best method on five of seven domain aggregates, with the same critic design for state and pixel inputs.

Path-coupled Bellman flows

PCBF changes the path a flow critic is trained on rather than the critic itself. A velocity network vθ(t,z∣s,a)v_\theta(t, z \mid s, a)vθ​(t,z∣s,a) is trained by flow matching, and a slowly updated copy vθ−v_{\theta^-}vθ−​ generates successor returns. Three steps turn one noise draw into a low-variance Bellman target.

  1. Share one noise draw

    The successor return is generated from the same noise that the current path will use, by integrating the target flow from t=0t = 0t=0 to t=1t = 1t=1.

  2. Build both paths from it

    Both paths leave the same point at t=0t = 0t=0 and end at Bellman-related samples at t=1t = 1t=1. Rewriting the current path exposes the Bellman geometry: the last term is a residual anchor that pins t=0t = 0t=0 to X0X_0X0​ for any γ\gammaγ, while t=1t = 1t=1 still gives the Bellman sample R+γX′R + \gamma X'R+γX′.

Acting with the learned critic

At deployment, a behaviour-cloned proposal policy samples K=16K = 16K=16 candidate actions. Each candidate is scored by the mean terminal return of the learned flow over MMM noise draws, and the agent executes the highest-scoring candidate.

What the analysis guarantees

The analysis identifies the velocity field that PCBF regresses onto, shows exactly where the λ-target's bias comes from, and explains why sharing noise keeps that bias small.

Correct endpointsProposition 5.3

The Bellman-interpolated marginals start at the prior and end at the distributional Bellman update: Ps,a,0=N(0,1)P_{s,a,0} = \mathcal{N}(0,1)Ps,a,0​=N(0,1) and Ps,a,1=(Tπη)s,aP_{s,a,1} = (\mathcal{T}^{\pi}\eta)_{s,a}Ps,a,1​=(Tπη)s,a​.

The velocity PCBF learnsTheorem 5.5

The population-optimal field is the posterior mean of the path velocity, and it transports the Bellman-interpolated marginals through the continuity equation ∂tPs,a+∂x(Ps,a vs,a⋆)=0\partial_t P_{s,a} + \partial_x(P_{s,a}\, v^{\star}_{s,a}) = 0∂t​Ps,a​+∂x​(Ps,a​vs,a⋆​)=0.

vs,a⋆(x,t)=E[(R+γX1′)−X0 ∣ Xt=x, S=s, A=a]v^{\star}_{s,a}(x,t) = \mathbb{E}\big[(R + \gamma X'_1) - X_0 \,\big|\, X_t = x,\, S = s,\, A = a\big]vs,a⋆​(x,t)=E[(R+γX1′​)−X0​​Xt​=x,S=s,A=a]
Where the λ-bias comes fromProposition 5.6

The regression learns vs,a(λ)=vs,a⋆+λ Bs,a[Cvˉ]v^{(\lambda)}_{s,a} = v^{\star}_{s,a} + \lambda\, \mathcal{B}_{s,a}[C_{\bar v}]vs,a(λ)​=vs,a⋆​+λBs,a​[Cvˉ​]. The control variate has zero mean given the successor interpolant, but the regression conditions on the current interpolant; that mismatch is the only source of λ-bias.

Distribution-free bias boundProposition 5.7

Without Gaussianity or deterministic rewards, the bias splits into successor-flow approximation error and an intrinsic cross-conditioning term, and it scales linearly in ∣λ∣|\lambda|∣λ∣.

∥vs,a(λ)(⋅,t)−vs,a⋆(⋅,t)∥L2(Ps,a,t)≤∣λ∣ (εapp+εint)\big\| v^{(\lambda)}_{s,a}(\cdot,t) - v^{\star}_{s,a}(\cdot,t) \big\|_{L^2(P_{s,a,t})} \le |\lambda|\,\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{app}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\big)​vs,a(λ)​(⋅,t)−vs,a⋆​(⋅,t)​L2(Ps,a,t​)​≤∣λ∣(εapp​+εint​)
Shared-noise contractionProposition 5.8

Comparing two return generators on the same transition and the same latent seed, the shared-noise Bellman update contracts by γ\gammaγ, and the coupled interpolants differ by at most tγt\gammatγ times the generator gap, so discrepancies vanish near the source.

Dp(TpcG, TpcH)≤γ Dp(G,H)D_p(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{pc}}G,\, \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{pc}}H) \le \gamma\, D_p(G, H)Dp​(Tpc​G,Tpc​H)≤γDp​(G,H)

If the ODE solver returns the successor endpoint with error δ\deltaδ, the target moves by at most (∣γ−λ∣+λLtt)∥δ∥\big(|\gamma - \lambda| + \lambda L_t t\big)\|\delta\|(∣γ−λ∣+λLt​t)∥δ∥, so a λ closer to γ\gammaγ reduces sensitivity whenever the successor field is smooth (Ltt<1L_t t < 1Lt​t<1).

Results

The evaluation asks two questions: does PCBF learn the right return law when the answer is known, and does a better critic translate into control on standard offline RL benchmarks?

It recovers known return laws

Three toy environments have return laws that are known in closed form or by exact Monte Carlo: Solitaire Dice, whose return is heavy-tailed and discrete; a Bernoulli MRP, whose return is exactly Uniform[0,2]\mathrm{Uniform}[0,2]Uniform[0,2]; and a Discrete Monte Carlo chain with multi-modal, long-horizon returns.

It holds up on 38 offline RL tasks

The benchmark covers four state-based OGBench domains, two pixel-based OGBench domains with 64×64×364 \times 64 \times 364×64×3 observations, and eight D4RL Adroit tasks for dexterous manipulation. Scores are averaged over eight seeds, or four for pixel-based tasks, and baselines span quantile critics, flow critics, and strong scalar methods.

Variance falls without the distribution drifting

Raising λ steadily lowers the spread of the Bellman velocity loss within a run. Raising the consistency weight in Value Flows, by contrast, systematically degrades distributional accuracy, whereas PCBF's Wasserstein error stays low across most of the λ range; on the Discrete MC chain it sits near 0.5 for every λ∈[0,0.95]\lambda \in [0, 0.95]λ∈[0,0.95]. On the Bernoulli MRP the error is lowest for λ≤0.3\lambda \le 0.3λ≤0.3 and rises as λ\lambdaλ approaches γ\gammaγ, which is the bias side of the trade-off.

λ is worth tuning, once per domain

The best λ differs across tasks: 0.2 on scene-play task 2 and puzzle-4x4 task 4, 0 on visual-antmaze task 1, and 0.5, 0.1, and 0.6 on the pen, relocate, and hammer expert tasks. The paper therefore tunes λ once per domain on a single task and reuses it for the rest.

Coupling also absorbs discretisation error

Training integrates the flow with a ten-step Euler solver, so the integrated paths drift from the closed-form PCBF interpolation. With shared noise, this corrected Bellman residual stays below the independent-noise ablation at every flow time and solver budget tested on Solitaire Dice, and on average by more than an order of magnitude.

Limitations

Flow critics are not free. Training and evaluation integrate an ODE, so PCBF costs about as much as Value Flows and roughly two and a half times a scalar critic in wall-clock time. Moreover, λ is task-dependent and is tuned once per domain; fully adaptive selection during training is left for future work.

Run it

The official JAX implementation builds on the FQL and Value Flows codebases and includes the toy environments and the baseline agents. Every experiment is one call to main.py, and the two PCBF-specific settings are the discount γ\gammaγ and the control weight λ\lambdaλ.

Install
conda create -n PCBF python=3.10.13 -y
conda activate PCBF
conda install -c conda-forge glew -y
conda install -c conda-forge mesalib -y
pip install -r requirements.txt
Train on one task
python main.py \
  --env_name=puzzle-4x4-play-singletask-task1-v0 \
  --agent=agents/lambda_flow.py \
  --agent.discount=0.99 \
  --agent.lambda_param=0.2 \
  --seed=0

Per-domain settings from the paper's Table 5. Within a domain, λ is tuned on one task and reused for the other four; Adroit tasks are tuned individually with γ=0.99\gamma = 0.99γ=0.99.
